title: MTH_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: Her SUMMARY slide defines a function as a relation that assigns
options: exactly one input to each output
every value of the codomain to some input
exactly one output to each input
equal numbers of inputs and outputs
questions.why: Why C is right: those are her words on slide 25, and both halves carry weight — every input is used, and none of them gets two outputs. Why the others are wrong: A states a stronger, separate property that x² already fails, since f(−3) = f(3) · B describes the codomain being fully used, which slide 5 shows is not required · D counts the two sets, which her x² diagram deliberately does not do.

questions.q: The domain of f(x) = (3x + 1)/(x² + 5) is
questions.why: Why A is right: she sets x² + 5 ≠ 0, so x² ≠ −5, and a square is never negative, so nothing has to be thrown out. Why the others are wrong: B solves x² − 5 = 0 instead; the slide's denominator is a sum, not a difference · C excludes the zero of the numerator, which only makes f(x) = 0 and is perfectly legal · D reads x² ≠ −5 as x ≠ −5, dropping the square.

questions.q: The range of f(x) = 2 − |x − 3| is
questions.why: Why D is right: from |x − 3| ≥ 0 she multiplies by −1, which reverses it to −|x − 3| ≤ 0, then adds 2 to get y ≤ 2. Why the others are wrong: A keeps the inequality pointing the same way after multiplying by −1 — the step she flags · B uses a round bracket at 2, but y = 2 is attained at x = 3 · C quotes the fact |x − 3| ≥ 0 without doing anything to it.

questions.q: The inverse of f(x) = 3x − 7 is
questions.why: Why B is right: let y = 3x − 7, switch x with y to get x = 3y − 7, then isolate y — her three named steps. Why the others are wrong: A gives the reciprocal; an inverse hands x back, a reciprocal hands back 1 · C adds nothing after switching, losing the sign when 7 crosses the equals sign · D multiplies by 3 instead of dividing, undoing the wrong operation.

questions.q: With f(x) = 5x − 4 and g(x) = x², g ∘ f =
questions.why: Why A is right: g ∘ f = g[f(x)] = (5x − 4)(5x − 4), and she shows both middle terms −20x and −20x before collecting them. Why the others are wrong: B is f ∘ g, the other composite on the same slide — order is part of the question · C squares each term separately and loses the middle terms entirely · D keeps only one of the two −20x terms.

questions.q: Slide 22 asks for f(x) = x + 2 at x = 0, 1, 2. The correct y-values are
questions.why: Why D is right: substitute: 0 + 2 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 2 = 4, giving the points (0, 2), (1, 3), (2, 4). Why the others are wrong: A is the table printed on the slide, and it is wrong — those are the values of 2 − x, which agrees with x + 2 only at x = 0 · B lists the inputs again instead of the outputs · C doubles each input rather than adding 2.

questions.q: TASK: the domain and range of h(x) = √(x + 2) − 8 are
questions.why: Why B is right: x + 2 ≥ 0 gives x ≥ −2, and √(x + 2) ≥ 0 gives √(x + 2) − 8 ≥ −8; both endpoints are attained at x = −2. Why the others are wrong: A uses round brackets, but h(−2) = −8 is a legal input with a real output · C solves x − 2 ≥ 0 instead of x + 2 ≥ 0 · D reverses the range inequality; nothing here was multiplied by a negative.

questions.q: For f(x) = x² − 4, f(3) =
questions.why: Why C is right: square first, then subtract: (3)² − 4 = 9 − 4 = 5, which is the order the slide spells out. Why the others are wrong: A subtracts first and squares afterwards, computing (3 − 4)² — a different function · B squares and forgets to subtract the 4 · D doubles the input instead of squaring it.

questions.q: For f(x) = ax² + bx + c, the constant c is
questions.why: Why D is right: putting x = 0 leaves c, so c is where the parabola cuts the y-axis. Why the others are wrong: A is the claim made on the slide, and it is wrong: the vertex sits at x = −b/2a, which is 0 only when b = 0 · B names a vertical line x = −b/2a, not a constant term · C is decided by the discriminant b² − 4ac, not by c alone.

questions.q: The vertex of f(x) = x² + 6x + 5 is at
questions.why: Why B is right: x = −b/2a = −6/2 = −3, and f(−3) = 9 − 18 + 5 = −4. Why the others are wrong: A drops the minus in −b/2a · C takes the constant term 5 as the vertex height instead of evaluating f(−3) · D uses −b rather than −b/2a, forgetting to divide by 2a.

questions.q: The equation x² − 4x + 7 = 0 has
options: two real roots of opposite sign
questions.why: Why C is right: Δ = (−4)² − 4(1)(7) = 16 − 28 = −12 < 0, so the parabola never meets the x-axis. Why the others are wrong: A would need Δ > 0 · B would need Δ = 0 exactly · D would need Δ > 0 and a negative constant term.

questions.q: Log₃ 81 equals
questions.why: Why A is right: a logarithm asks for the exponent, and 3⁴ = 81. Why the others are wrong: B is 81/3, dividing instead of taking the exponent · C quotes the base back · D is √81, which answers a different question.

questions.q: Which function models exponential decay?
questions.why: Why B is right: the base lies strictly between 0 and 1, so successive powers shrink. Why the others are wrong: A has base greater than 1, so it grows · C is a power function — the variable is in the base, not the exponent · D is the inverse of an exponential, not an exponential.

questions.q: The solution set of |x − 3| < 5 is
questions.why: Why C is right: the inequality unfolds to −5 < x − 3 < 5, and adding 3 throughout gives −2 < x < 8. Why the others are wrong: A keeps only the upper half and forgets the lower bound · B solves the inequality with > instead of <, giving the outside of the interval · D never adds the 3 back.

questions.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≤ 0 and f(x) = x² − 3 for x > 0, then f(0) is
questions.why: Why A is right: x = 0 satisfies x ≤ 0, so the first branch applies: 2(0) + 1 = 1. Why the others are wrong: B uses the second branch, but x > 0 excludes 0 · C would break the one-output rule; the branches are on disjoint intervals · D assumes a gap at the boundary, but x ≤ 0 covers x = 0.

questions.q: Lim x→2 (x³ − 3)/(x² − 6) equals
questions.why: Why D is right: substitution gives (8 − 3)/(4 − 6) = 5/(−2), a well-defined expression, so the work is finished. Why the others are wrong: A loses the sign of the denominator 4 − 6 = −2 · B treats a negative denominator as a failure, but only 0/0 stops substitution · C reads the negative denominator as zero.

questions.q: Lim x→2 (1/x − 1/2)/(x − 2) equals
questions.why: Why A is right: multiply top and bottom by 2x to get (2 − x)/[2x(x − 2)], write 2 − x = −1(x − 2), cancel, then substitute. Why the others are wrong: B cancels 2 − x against x − 2 directly, which flips the sign — the error the slide's −1 step exists to prevent · C substitutes x = 2 into −1/x instead of −1/(2x) · D makes both mistakes at once.

questions.q: TASK: lim x→3 (x³ − 27)/(x − 3) equals
questions.why: Why C is right: x³ − 27 = (x − 3)(x² + 3x + 9); cancel and substitute to get 9 + 9 + 9 = 27, which L'Hôpital confirms as 3x² at x = 3. Why the others are wrong: A reads the 0/0 from substitution as the answer, but 0/0 decides nothing · B keeps only the x² term of the quadratic factor · D quotes the point being approached instead of the limit.

questions.q: Lim x→0 (√(x + 9) − 3)/x equals
questions.why: Why B is right: multiply by the conjugate of the numerator, √(x + 9) + 3, leaving x/[x(√(x + 9) + 3)]; cancel x and substitute. Why the others are wrong: A reads the 0/0 from substitution as zero · C cancels the 3 in the denominator against only one term · D inverts the final fraction 1/(3 + 3).

questions.q: Lim x→∞ x²/eˣ equals
questions.why: Why D is right: one application of L'Hôpital gives 2x/eˣ, still ∞/∞, so differentiate again to reach 2/eˣ, and the exponential drives it to 0. Why the others are wrong: A assumes the polynomial wins; the exponential grows faster · B stops after checking that top and bottom both grow · C reads off the numerator of 2/eˣ and forgets the denominator.

questions.q: Applying L'Hôpital's Rule to lim f(x)/g(x) replaces it with
questions.why: Why D is right: top and bottom are differentiated separately, which is why she names f and g and differentiates each on its own line. Why the others are wrong: A is the quotient rule; if a g² appears in your working you used the wrong rule · B multiplies the derivatives instead of dividing them · C differentiates the whole quotient, which is the quotient rule again.

questions.q: Slide 23 states 5 − x³ ≤ f(x) ≤ 5 − x³ and asks for lim x→0 f(x). The corrected bound and the limit are
options: upper bound 5 + x³; the limit is 5
upper bound 5 − x³; the limit is 5
upper bound 5 + x³; the limit is 0
upper bound 5 + x³; the limit is 10
questions.why: Why A is right: the theorem line one row above gives the bounds as 5 − x³ and 5 + x³, so the printed upper bound is a misprint; both bounds tend to 5, so f is squeezed to 5. Why the others are wrong: B keeps the misprint, which would make the two bounds identical and the hypothesis vacuous · C reads off x³ at 0 instead of the whole bound · D adds the two bounds instead of noting they agree.

questions.q: Which two of her ten limit properties carry a non-zero proviso?
questions.why: Why C is right: the Quotient property needs lim g(x) ≠ 0 and the Reciprocal property needs lim f(x) ≠ 0 — exactly the condition that fails in a 0/0 problem. Why the others are wrong: A the Product property needs nothing; both limits may be anything · B both hold with no condition at all · D the Power property is unconditional in her statement.

questions.q: TASK: lim x→4 (1/√x − 1/2)/(x − 4) equals
questions.why: Why B is right: clear the small fractions with 2√x to get (2 − √x)/[2√x(x − 4)], factor x − 4 as (√x − 2)(√x + 2), write 2 − √x = −1(√x − 2), cancel and substitute. Why the others are wrong: A cancels 2 − √x against √x − 2 without the −1 rewrite, the same slip as slide 7 · C forgets one factor of 2 when substituting into 2√x(√x + 2) · D quotes the answer to the slide-7 example instead.

questions.q: The three conditions for f to be continuous at c are
options: f(c) is defined and f′(c) exists
f(c) is defined, the limit exists, and they are equal
the limit exists and is finite
f is defined on both sides of c
questions.why: Why B is right: all three in that order; failing any one makes f discontinuous at c. Why the others are wrong: A asks for a derivative, which continuity does not require · C is condition (ii) only, and says nothing about f(c) · D is weaker than any of the three and permits a break at c.

questions.q: On a graph, the left limit at x = 2 is 3, the right limit is −4, and a solid dot sits at (2, 1). Then lim x→2 f(x) is
questions.why: Why D is right: a two-sided limit exists only when the two one-sided limits agree, and 3 ≠ −4. Why the others are wrong: A quotes f(2), the solid dot, which the limit never inspects · B reports the left-hand limit alone · C reports the right-hand limit alone.

questions.q: For that same graph — left limit 3, right limit −4, solid dot at (2, 1), open circles at (2, 3) and (2, −4) — the value f(2) is
questions.why: Why A is right: only a shaded dot may be quoted as a function value; the open circles mark heights the curve approaches but never takes. Why the others are wrong: B reads an open circle as a function value · C reads the other open circle as a function value · D ignores the solid dot; a function can be defined at a point and still be discontinuous there.

questions.q: For f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1), the limit as x → 1 is
questions.why: Why C is right: factor and cancel to get x + 1 for every x ≠ 1, so both one-sided limits are 2 — even though f(1) itself is undefined. Why the others are wrong: A reads the 0/0 from substitution as the answer · B concludes from f(1) being undefined, but a limit never uses the value at the point · D substitutes into the denominator's factor instead of x + 1.

questions.q: At x = 0 the function g(x) = |x| is
questions.why: Why C is right: the left and right limits are both 0 and g(0) = 0, so all three conditions hold; continuity is about not lifting the pen, not about smoothness. Why the others are wrong: A confuses a corner with a break in the curve · B is false: |0| = 0 · D misreads the superscript + as part of the function.

questions.q: If lim x→3⁺ f(x) = +∞ and lim x→3⁻ f(x) = −∞, then
options: the two-sided limit does not exist and x = 3 is a vertical asymptote
the limit is 0, since +∞ and −∞ cancel
questions.why: Why B is right: ∞ is not a real number, so writing lim = +∞ describes how the limit fails rather than giving it a value. Why the others are wrong: A treats ∞ as a value the limit takes · C adds two things that are not numbers · D would need f(3) defined and equal to a finite limit.

questions.q: Which statement about lim x→c f(x) and f(c) is correct?
options: if f(c) is defined then the limit exists
if the limit exists then f is continuous at c
the limit is built only from x near c, never from x = c
questions.why: Why D is right: cover the point x = c with your thumb: anything still readable is the limit, anything hidden is f(c). Why the others are wrong: A holds only when f is continuous at c, which is the thing being tested · B is false at a break, where f(c) is defined and the two sides disagree · C skips conditions (i) and (iii); f(c) may be missing or at the wrong height.

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = 3x¹⁰⁰ − 4x is
questions.why: Why A is right: (3×100)x⁹⁹ for the first term, and 4x differentiates to 4·1·x⁰ = 4, since x⁰ = 1 — the line she writes out separately. Why the others are wrong: B loses the second term altogether · C stops one step early; x⁰ is 1, so the term is just −4 · D drops the power down without multiplying by the old power 100.

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = (4x + 6)(2x³ − 5x) is
questions.why: Why B is right: u v′ + u′ v = (4x + 6)(6x² − 5) + (2x³ − 5x)(4), and expanding the product first confirms it. Why the others are wrong: A is the answer printed on the slide, and it is wrong — it is not the derivative of anything on that slide · C follows the slide's other misprint, where the square on 6x² was dropped · D multiplies the two derivatives, u′v′, which is not the product rule.

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = x/cos(x) is
questions.why: Why A is right: v u′ − u v′ over v² gives [cos x·1 − x(−sin x)]/cos²x, and the double negative turns −x sin x into +x sin x. Why the others are wrong: B is the slide's printed final line, which drops the factor x from the second term · C forgets that cos differentiates to −sin, so only one minus appears · D reverses the numerator's order, which negates the whole answer.

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = (6x − 3)/(5x²) is
questions.why: Why C is right: [5x²·6 − (6x − 3)·10x]/(5x²)² = (−30x² + 30x)/25x⁴, and dividing top and bottom by 5x gives 6(1 − x)/5x³. Why the others are wrong: A subtracts (6x − 3)(10x) without changing the sign of −30x, so +30x becomes −30x · B reverses the numerator terms, negating the answer · D differentiates numerator and denominator separately.

questions.q: The derivative of f(x) = cos(x²) is
questions.why: Why D is right: y′(u)·u′(x) with y = cos u and u = x² gives −sin(u)·2x, then u is replaced by x². Why the others are wrong: A forgets the inner derivative 2x · B loses the minus that comes from cos differentiating to −sin · C leaves the answer in u instead of putting the inside function back.

questions.q: TASK 1: the derivative of f(x) = (2x − 4)² is
questions.why: Why C is right: with u = 2x − 4, y′(u)·u′(x) = 2u·2 = 4(2x − 4); expanding first gives 4x² − 16x + 16, whose derivative is the same. Why the others are wrong: A is 2(2x − 4) — the inner derivative 2 was never paid, which is the whole point of the task · B just drops the square and copies the bracket · D differentiates the expansion but mishandles the middle term.

questions.q: Differentiating x² + y² = 25 implicitly gives dy/dx =
questions.why: Why D is right: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0 because d(y²)/dx = 2y·dy/dx, and the constant 25 differentiates to 0. Why the others are wrong: A loses the sign when moving 2x across the equals sign · B cancels only the 2 in the denominator · C cancels only the 2 in the numerator.

questions.q: Differentiating xy + 6x⁴ = y implicitly gives dy/dx =
questions.why: Why A is right: the product rule on xy gives y + x(dy/dx); collect the dy/dx terms, factorise to (dy/dx)(x − 1), then divide. Why the others are wrong: B loses the sign when 24x³ and y are moved to the other side · C forgets the y produced by the product rule on xy and changes its sign · D drops the y term completely, treating xy as if only x were differentiated.

questions.q: For x(t) = 2t + 1 and y(t) = t² − t, dy/dx =
questions.why: Why B is right: her parametric rule is dy/dx = dy/dt ÷ dx/dt, with dy/dt = 2t − 1 and dx/dt = 2; leaving the answer in t is correct. Why the others are wrong: A quotes dy/dt, which is not the gradient of the curve · C divides the wrong way round · D divides by x(t) instead of by dx/dt.

questions.q: Differentiating y = √x from first principles gives
questions.why: Why A is right: multiply by the conjugate so the numerator becomes h, cancel h, then let h → 0 inside the surd to get 1/(√x + √x). Why the others are wrong: B cancels the root as well as the h · C inverts the final fraction · D puts h = 0 in only one of the two roots in the denominator.

questions.q: For f(x, y) = 3x² + 2xy − y³, the partial derivative ∂f/∂y is
questions.why: Why B is right: x is held constant, so 3x² dies, 2xy leaves 2x, and −y³ gives −3y². Why the others are wrong: A is ∂f/∂x — and note the slide labels the second answer ∂f/∂x as well, which is a misprint · C loses the minus sign already sitting in front of y³ · D differentiates by both variables at once.

questions.q: The first derivative of f(x) = x⁴ + 2x³ − 15x + 4 is
questions.why: Why D is right: term by term, and the constant 4 differentiates to 0 — the NOTE she puts in bold on that slide. Why the others are wrong: A keeps the constant, which should vanish · B leaves the x on the −15 term; the power rule with n = 1 gives 15x⁰ = 15 · C forgets to multiply 2x³ by its old power 3.

questions.q: The second derivative of f(x) = √(x³) is
questions.why: Why C is right: rewrite as x^(3/2), differentiate to (3/2)x^(1/2), then differentiate again: the coefficients multiply to 3/4 and the exponent falls to −1/2. Why the others are wrong: A stops at the first derivative · B multiplies the coefficients but does not lower the exponent · D lowers the exponent but forgets to multiply by the 1/2 that came down.

questions.q: For f(x) = ln x, the value of f‴(2) is
questions.why: Why D is right: y′ = x⁻¹, y″ = −x⁻², y‴ = 2x⁻³, so f‴(2) = 2/8 = 1/4. Why the others are wrong: A uses 1/x³ and forgets the coefficient 2 that the second differentiation produced · B keeps the minus from the second derivative, but the third flips it back · C quotes the coefficient of x⁻³ instead of evaluating at 2.

questions.q: The third derivative of sin(5x) + e³ˣ is
questions.why: Why C is right: the chain rule deposits another 5 and another 3 at every step: 5, 25, 125 and 3, 9, 27, while cos → −sin → −cos supplies the minus. Why the others are wrong: A collects the chain factor only once instead of at every differentiation · B loses the sign that the trigonometric cycle produces · D attaches the minus to the exponential too, but eᵘ never changes sign.

questions.q: TASK 1: the second derivative of y = cos(3x) is
questions.why: Why B is right: y′ = −3 sin(3x), then y″ = −3·3 cos(3x); the sign arrives at the first step and the second adds none. Why the others are wrong: A misses the minus produced when cos differentiates to −sin · C collects the chain factor 3 only once · D stops the trigonometric cycle one step early.

questions.q: The notation f⁽⁴⁾(x) means
questions.why: Why A is right: from the fourth order on, the prime marks are replaced by a bracketed superscript, which counts differentiations. Why the others are wrong: B reads the bracketed superscript as an exponent — exactly what the brackets exist to prevent · C confuses a superscript counter with an argument · D combines both misreadings.

questions.q: The second derivative of ln(1 + x²) is
questions.why: Why C is right: the chain rule gives f′ = 2x/(1 + x²), which is a quotient, so the quotient rule gives [(1 + x²)2 − 2x(2x)]/(1 + x²)², and she expands the denominator. Why the others are wrong: A adds the two numerator terms instead of subtracting, ignoring v u′ − u v′ · B differentiates only the numerator of f′ and leaves the denominator alone · D squares the denominator without applying the quotient rule at all.

questions.q: Her Example 1 concludes that ∫2x dx equals
questions.why: Why A is right: x² is not the only antiderivative of 2x: adding any constant changes nothing when you differentiate, so the whole family must be reported. Why the others are wrong: B is an incomplete answer, and the whole example exists to stop this · C multiplies by the power instead of dividing by the new one · D divides the coefficient by the old power rather than using the power rule.

questions.q: ∫x⁴dx equals
questions.why: Why B is right: raise the power by one and divide by the new power, then add c. Why the others are wrong: A differentiates instead of integrating · C multiplies by the new power rather than dividing · D raises the power but forgets to divide.

questions.q: ∫(2/x⁷)dx equals
questions.why: Why D is right: rewrite as 2x⁻⁷, so the new exponent is −6 and you divide by −6: 2/(−6) = −1/3. Why the others are wrong: A keeps the answer positive, forgetting that dividing by −6 flips the sign · B lowers the exponent instead of raising it · C divides the coefficient but never changes the power.

questions.q: ∫(11x¹⁰ − 4x⁹ + 1)dx equals
questions.why: Why B is right: split term by term; 11/11 = 1, 4/10 = 2/5, and ∫1dx = x by the power rule with n = 0. Why the others are wrong: A drops ∫1dx, treating the constant term as if it integrated to nothing · C leaves the 1 unintegrated · D differentiates the polynomial instead of integrating it.

questions.q: The power rule for integration excludes n = −1 because
options: x⁻¹ has no antiderivative at all
n + 1 = 0, so you would divide by zero
questions.why: Why D is right: the rule divides by the new power, and at n = −1 that new power is 0. Why the others are wrong: A is false — it simply is not given by this rule · B confuses the sign of the exponent with the validity of the rule · C is false: x⁰ = 1.

questions.q: ∫₀³ 4x dx equals
questions.why: Why C is right: F(x) = 2x², so the value is 2(3²) − 2(0²) = 18; the coefficient 2 is factored outside the evaluation. Why the others are wrong: A substitutes into f rather than F, giving 4(3) − 4(0) · B forgets to divide by the new power, using 4x² as the antiderivative · D integrates to x² and drops the coefficient.

questions.q: ∫₋₁⁵ (3x² − 6)dx equals
questions.why: Why A is right: x³ from −1 to 5 is 125 − (−1) = 126, and 6x from −1 to 5 is 6(5 − (−1)) = 36, so 126 − 36 = 90. Why the others are wrong: B takes (−1)³ as +1, giving 125 − 1 = 124 for the first bracket · C reads 5 − (−1) as 4, so the second bracket becomes 24 · D computes the first bracket and forgets to subtract the second.

questions.q: ∫₂³ (1/x²)dx equals
questions.why: Why A is right: rewrite as x⁻², so F(x) = −1/x, and −(1/3 − 1/2) = −(−1/6) = 1/6. Why the others are wrong: B loses the minus in F(x) = −1/x, so the bracket is never negated · C adds 1/2 and 1/3 instead of subtracting · D integrates x⁻² as x⁻¹ without dividing by the new power.

questions.q: TASK 2: ∫₋₁² (7x − 5)dx equals
questions.why: Why C is right: F(x) = 7x²/2 − 5x, so F(2) = 4 and F(−1) = 7/2 + 5 = 17/2, and 4 − 17/2 = −9/2; a negative value is legitimate for a signed integral. Why the others are wrong: A computes F(−1) − F(2), reversing the order of the limits · B adds the two values instead of subtracting · D reads −5(−1) as −5, losing the sign at the lower limit.

questions.q: Slide 7 states the substitution formula as
questions.why: Why D is right: it is the chain rule read backwards: spot an inner function and its derivative multiplying it. Why the others are wrong: A leaves the outer function differentiated, so nothing was integrated · B substitutes the derivative of the inner function into f · C multiplies by the inner function, which no rule licenses.

questions.q: Example 1: with u = x + 2, ∫₀²(x + 2)³dx equals
questions.why: Why B is right: the limits convert to u = 2 and u = 4, giving (1/4)(4⁴ − 2⁴) = (256 − 16)/4 = 60. Why the others are wrong: A computes 4⁴ − 2⁴ and forgets the factor 1/4 · C uses only the upper limit, 4⁴/4 · D evaluates 2⁴ alone, as if the lower limit were the answer.

questions.q: Slide 8 leaves ∫2x·e^(x²)dx as eᵘ + C. The complete answer is
questions.why: Why D is right: this is an indefinite integral, so u — which was your own invention — must be eliminated; u = x² puts it back. Why the others are wrong: A is what the slide prints, and it is incomplete: u does not appear in the question · B substitutes the derivative 2x into the exponent instead of u = x² · C multiplies by u as well as substituting it.

questions.q: ∫x·eˣ dx equals
questions.why: Why B is right: with u = x and dv = eˣdx, uv − ∫v du = x·eˣ − ∫eˣdx; differentiating the answer returns x·eˣ. Why the others are wrong: A adds the leftover integral instead of subtracting it · C is the result of the reverse choice u = eˣ, which raises the power of x instead of lowering it · D subtracts in the wrong order, negating the answer.

questions.q: ∫3x²·sin(x)dx equals
options: −3x²cos x + 6(x sin x + cos x) + C
3x²cos x − 6(x sin x + cos x) + C
−3x²cos x − 6(x sin x + cos x) + C
questions.why: Why A is right: dv = sin x dx gives v = −cos x, which is where the first minus comes from; the leftover −∫−cos x(6x dx) becomes +6∫x cos x dx, and that second pass gives x sin x + cos x. Why the others are wrong: B takes v = +cos x, reversing every sign in the answer · C misses that two minus signs make the leftover integral positive · D stops the second pass before integrating −∫sin x dx to +cos x.

questions.q: TASK 2: ∫x·ln(x)dx equals
questions.why: Why C is right: here u must be ln x and dv = x dx, because dv has to be something you can integrate; then ∫(x²/2)(1/x)dx = (1/2)∫x dx. Why the others are wrong: A forgets the 1/2 in front of the leftover ∫x dx · B adds the leftover integral instead of subtracting it · D quotes the standard integral of ln x, ignoring the extra factor of x.

questions.q: ∫√(1 − x²)dx equals
questions.why: Why B is right: x = sin u kills the root via 1 − sin²u = cos²u, then cos²u = (1 + cos 2u)/2 gives u/2 + sin(2u)/4, and sin 2u = 2 sin u cos u converts back to x. Why the others are wrong: A leaves half the answer in u; the substitution must be undone · C inverts the wrong function; x = sin u means u = sin⁻¹(x) · D drops both halves' factor of 1/2, which came from the double-angle identity.

questions.q: Slide 16 rewrites √(4 − 9x²) as 2√(1 − (3x/2)²) and sets 3x/2 = sin u. Then dx equals
questions.why: Why C is right: differentiating gives (3/2)dx = cos u du, so dx is cos u du multiplied by the reciprocal of 3/2. Why the others are wrong: A uses 3/2 instead of its reciprocal — the standard way to lose this question · B ignores the inner coefficient entirely, as if the substitution were x = sin u · D differentiates sin u to sin u.

questions.q: ∫[1/(x² + 3x)]dx equals
questions.why: Why D is right: factor to 1/(x(x + 3)), split as A/x + B/(x + 3), clear to 1 = A(x + 3) + Bx, then x = 0 gives A = 1/3 and x = −3 gives B = −1/3. Why the others are wrong: A misses that B came out negative · B treats the whole denominator as if the numerator were its derivative · C recombines the logs as a product, which corresponds to A = B = 1/3.

questions.q: In 7x − 6 = A(x + 3) + B(x − 2), the value of B is
questions.why: Why A is right: set x = −3, the root that kills A: 7(−3) − 6 = −27 and B(−3 − 2) = −5B, so −27 = −5B and two negatives give B = 27/5. Why the others are wrong: B divides −27 by +5, missing that x − 2 is also negative at x = −3 · C forgets to divide by the factor −5 at all · D swaps in the value of A and negates it.

questions.q: A definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx is improper if
options: a limit of integration is infinite, or f has a discontinuity on [a, b]
the integrand is negative somewhere on [a, b]
the answer is not a whole number
the interval [a, b] is very long
questions.why: Why A is right: those are her two triggers, and you must check for both before starting. Why the others are wrong: B describes a signed integral, which is perfectly ordinary · C confuses the value with the type of integral · D a finite interval of any length is not improper on its own.

questions.q: The first line of any Type I answer is
questions.why: Why D is right: the symbol has no meaning until the infinite limit is replaced by a letter; marks are given for writing this line. Why the others are wrong: A substitutes ∞ into an antiderivative, but ∞ is not a number you may substitute · B leaves the upper limit at ∞ and reuses x as the limit variable · C reverses the order of the limits as well.

questions.q: ∫₀^∞ xe⁻ˣ dx
questions.why: Why C is right: the antiderivative is −xe⁻ˣ − e⁻ˣ; the lower limit contributes +1, and −te⁻ᵗ is −∞/∞, so L'Hôpital sends it to 0. Why the others are wrong: A assumes −te⁻ᵗ runs to −∞, but the exponential beats the polynomial · B forgets the +1 that subtracting the value at t = 0 contributes · D loses the sign when the lower-limit value −1 is subtracted.

options: diverges, because one half already runs to infinity
converges, since the two halves cancel
diverges only if both halves diverge
questions.why: Why B is right: the sum formula applies only if both halves converge, so once the piece from 0 to ∞ is unbounded the question is over. Why the others are wrong: A tries to cancel two infinities, which the definition forbids · C makes the same cancellation error · D reverses the hypothesis: both halves must converge, not just one.

questions.q: ∫₋₁² (1/x⁴)dx
options: diverges; the integrand is undefined at x = 0, which lies inside the interval
questions.why: Why C is right: split at 0 and take one-sided limits; both pieces run to +∞, so the integral diverges. Why the others are wrong: A applies the Fundamental Theorem straight across, giving a negative number for a strictly positive integrand · B takes the magnitude of that same illegal calculation · D keeps only the value at the upper limit.

questions.q: With 0 ≤ g(x) ≤ f(x) for all x ≥ a, which conclusion is valid?
questions.why: Why B is right: in her lettering g is underneath and f is on top, so the big one convergent drags the small one down with it. Why the others are wrong: A argues upward from the small function, which proves nothing · C argues downward from the big function, which also proves nothing · D contradicts the inequality outright.

options: converges to a value you can compute
questions.why: Why A is right: x³ + 7 ≥ x³ gives √(x³ + 7) ≥ √(x³), and taking reciprocals reverses it, so the integrand is at most x^(−3/2), where p = 3/2 > 1. Why the others are wrong: B carries the inequality through the reciprocal without reversing it · C comparison delivers a verdict, never a number · D the comparison lands in a useful direction, so it does decide it.

questions.q: For x ≥ 3, √(x² − 1) < x. It follows that 1/√(x² − 1) is
options: less than 1/x, so the integral converges
greater than 1/x, so the integral converges
less than 1/x, so the integral diverges
greater than 1/x, so the integral diverges
questions.why: Why D is right: reciprocals of positive numbers reverse the inequality, and ∫₃^∞ dx/x has p = 1, which Note 1 places on the divergent side. Why the others are wrong: A keeps the inequality pointing the same way through the reciprocal · B gets the inequality right but reads p = 1 as convergent · C gets both halves wrong and reaches the right verdict by accident.

questions.q: If f(x) ≤ 0 on [a, b], the area between y = f(x) and the x-axis is
questions.why: Why D is right: below the axis every strip contributes a negative amount, so the integral is negative and an area cannot be. Why the others are wrong: A is the first case of the rule, for f ≥ 0, and would report a negative area · B substitutes the limits into f instead of into an antiderivative · C adds a constant of integration to a definite integral, which never carries one.

questions.q: Example 1: the area between f(x) = 5x − x² and the x-axis is
questions.why: Why A is right: set f(x) = 0 to get x = 0 and x = 5, test f(2) = 6 > 0, then [5x²/2 − x³/3]₀⁵ = 125/2 − 125/3 = 125/6 ≈ 20.83. Why the others are wrong: B keeps the first term of the antiderivative and drops the cubic one · C keeps the cubic term and drops the first · D evaluates lower minus upper, reversing the limits.

questions.q: Example 2: the area bounded by f(x) = x² − 1, the x-axis, x = 0 and x = 2 is
questions.why: Why B is right: the curve cuts the axis at x = 1, inside [0, 2], so split there: |∫₀¹| + ∫₁² = 2/3 + 4/3 = 2. Why the others are wrong: A is the unsplit integral ∫₀²(x² − 1)dx, which lets the two pieces partly cancel · C is the piece above the axis only · D is the first piece with the modulus omitted.

questions.q: TASK 1: the area between f(x) = 6x − x² and the x-axis is
questions.why: Why C is right: 6x − x² = 0 gives x = 0 and x = 6; f(3) = 9 > 0, so no modulus, and [3x² − x³/3]₀⁶ = 108 − 72 = 36. Why the others are wrong: A reports the 216/3 term alone · B reports 3(6)² alone, dropping the cubic term · D integrates only as far as the vertex x = 3 instead of the root x = 6.

questions.q: The curves y = 3 − x and y = x² − 9 meet at
questions.why: Why A is right: 3 − x = x² − 9 rearranges to x² + x − 12 = 0, i.e. (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0. Why the others are wrong: B solves x² − 9 = 0, using one curve only · C reads the signs of the factors backwards · D takes x = 0 as an intersection, which it is not.

questions.q: The area bounded by y = 3 − x and y = x² − 9 is
questions.why: Why B is right: the integrand is (3 − x) − (x² − 9) = 12 − x − x², and 45/2 − (−104/3) = 343/6 ≈ 57.17. Why the others are wrong: A computes 45/2 − 104/3, failing to double the minus when subtracting a negative value · C is the upper-limit value alone · D is the magnitude of the lower-limit value alone.

questions.q: For f(x) = 2 − x and g(x) = 4 − x², the correct integrand for the enclosed area is
questions.why: Why C is right: at the test point x = 1, f(1) = 1 and g(1) = 3, so g is on top and is written first — the order comes from the test, not from which was named first. Why the others are wrong: A subtracts in the order the functions were named, giving −4.5 · B repairs the wrong order with a modulus, which she never uses between two curves · D adds the curves, which measures nothing.

questions.q: The area between y = sin x and y = cos x for 0 ≤ x ≤ π/2 is
questions.why: Why D is right: they cross where tan x = 1, at x = π/4; cos is on top before it and sin after it, so A₁ + A₂ = 4/√2 − 2. Why the others are wrong: A is the single unsplit integral, in which the two congruent lobes cancel exactly · B is A₁ only, half the region · C reverses the sign, giving a negative area.

questions.q: TASK: revolving f(x) = √x about the x-axis for 1 ≤ x ≤ 4 gives a volume of
questions.why: Why C is right: the disc formula squares the radius, so [√x]² = x and V = π[x²/2]₁⁴ = π(8 − 1/2). Why the others are wrong: A integrates √x itself, forgetting that the disc integrand is squared · B divides by 4 instead of 2 when integrating x · D uses the upper limit only.

questions.q: Revolving the region between y = x² and y = x⁵ on [0, 1] about the x-axis gives
questions.why: Why D is right: the washer subtracts the squares: π∫₀¹(x⁴ − x¹⁰)dx = π(1/5 − 1/11) = 6π/55. Why the others are wrong: A squares the difference of the radii, π∫(R − r)²dx, instead of subtracting the squares · B keeps only the x⁴ term · C drops the factor 6 that 1/5 − 1/11 produces.

questions.q: Revolving the region bounded by x = y², x = 3 and y = 0 about the y-axis gives
questions.why: Why B is right: R(y) = 3 is constant and r(y) = y², so π∫₀^√3 (9 − y⁴)dy = π[9y − y⁵/5]₀^√3. Why the others are wrong: A runs y from −√3 to √3, doubling the region she actually uses · C forgets to divide y⁵ by 5 · D keeps the 9y term and drops the y⁵/5 term.

questions.q: Revolving y = 2x² − x³, y = 0 about the y-axis by shells gives
questions.why: Why A is right: V = 2π∫₀²x(2x² − x³)dx = 2π[x⁴/2 − x⁵/5]₀² = 2π(8/5). Why the others are wrong: B drops the factor 2 in 2π, which is the unrolled shell's circumference · C doubles the answer a second time · D divides by 5 twice.

questions.q: Rotating the region under y = √x from 0 to 1 about the x-axis by shells gives
questions.why: Why B is right: the strip is horizontal, so the radius is y and the height is 1 − y²; V = 2π∫₀¹(y − y³)dy = 2π(1/2 − 1/4), which the disc method confirms. Why the others are wrong: A forgets the outer factor 2 · C uses y² as the strip height instead of 1 − y² · D doubles the value by taking the height as 1 + y².

questions.q: TASK: rotating the region under y = x² on [0, 2] about the line y = −1 gives
questions.why: Why A is right: the axis has moved, so R = x² + 1 and r = 1; π∫₀²(x⁴ + 2x²)dx = π(32/5 + 16/3). Why the others are wrong: B uses R = x² and r = 0, as if the axis were still the x-axis · C keeps only the x⁴ term after shifting · D mishandles the common denominator when adding 32/5 and 16/3.

questions.q: Slide 13 says the shell method integrates along an axis parallel to the axis of revolution. In fact the variable of integration runs
options: parallel to the axis of revolution
in either direction, since it makes no difference
perpendicular to the axis of revolution
questions.why: Why D is right: both her own examples show it: Example 1 revolves about the y-axis and integrates dx, Example 2 revolves about the x-axis and integrates dy. Why the others are wrong: A is what the slide prints, and her two examples contradict it · B describes the disc and washer methods, not shells · C would give the wrong radius and the wrong height.

questions.q: Revolving the region between x = y² + 1 and x = 3 about the line x = 3 gives
questions.why: Why C is right: R(y) = 3 − (y² + 1) = 2 − y², and setting y² + 1 = 3 gives limits ±√2; π∫(4 − 4y² + y⁴)dy = 64√2π/15. Why the others are wrong: A evaluates at y = √2 only, forgetting that subtracting the value at −√2 doubles it · B divides y⁵ by 5 but never divides the other terms correctly · D drops the √2 that (√2)³ and (√2)⁵ produce.

questions.q: For v(t) = 2t² + 6t + 1 km/h, the distance travelled in the first 5 hours is
questions.why: Why D is right: integrate the rate over the interval: [2t³/3 + 3t² + t]₀⁵ = 83.33 + 75 + 5. Why the others are wrong: A is v(5), the speed at the end, not the distance covered · B keeps the 2t³/3 term and drops the rest · C mishandles 250/3 as 86 rather than 83.33.

questions.q: For v(t) = 6t² − 6t − 12 with x(0) = −4, the net displacement over the first 5 seconds is
questions.why: Why C is right: a definite integral, so the constant cancels: [2t³ − 3t² − 12t]₀⁵ = 250 − 75 − 60. Why the others are wrong: A carries the −4 into the definite integral and subtracts it only once — this is x(5), the position, not the change in position · B is the total distance travelled, which she neither asks for nor teaches · D counts only the forward stretch after t = 2.

questions.q: The weight density of water used in the fluid-force integral is
questions.why: Why A is right: ρg = (1000)(9.8) = 9800, and kg/m³ multiplied by m/s² gives newtons per cubic metre. Why the others are wrong: B is the unit printed on the slide, and it is wrong — the number is right, the unit is not · C quotes the density ρ without multiplying by g · D quotes g without multiplying by ρ.

questions.q: Pulling up a 60 m rope of mass 66 g/m takes work equal to
questions.why: Why B is right: F(x) = 9.8(0.066)(60 − x) = 0.6468(60 − x), and ∫₀⁶⁰F dx = 0.6468(3600 − 1800). Why the others are wrong: A treats the force as constant at its starting value, but it falls to zero as the rope comes up · C leaves the mass in grams instead of converting to kilograms · D reports the initial force in newtons rather than the work done.

questions.q: With MR = 100 + 20Q + 3Q² and TR(2) = 260, the constant of integration is
questions.why: Why C is right: TR(Q) = 100Q + 10Q² + Q³ + C, and TR(2) = 200 + 40 + 8 + C = 248 + C, so 248 + C = 260. Why the others are wrong: A copies the given value straight into C instead of solving for it · B reports the value of the polynomial at Q = 2 rather than the constant · D solves 248 + C = 260 with the sign reversed.

questions.q: The capital growth ∫₄⁹ 6√t dt equals
questions.why: Why A is right: 6∫t^(1/2)dt = 4t^(3/2), and 4(27) − 4(8) = 108 − 32. Why the others are wrong: B is the answer printed on the slide, and it is wrong — it is the coefficient of t^(3/2) left stranded where the answer belongs · C is I(9) − I(4) = 18 − 12, substituting into the integrand instead of the antiderivative · D evaluates at the upper limit and forgets to subtract the lower one.

questions.q: With D(Q) = 1000 − 25Q and S(Q) = 100 + Q², the consumer surplus is
questions.why: Why D is right: equilibrium first: Q₀ = 20 and P₀ = 500, then CS = ∫₀²⁰(500 − 25Q)dQ = 10000 − 5000. Why the others are wrong: A is the producer surplus, ∫₀²⁰(400 − Q²)dQ — the two are close enough that swapping them looks plausible · B keeps 500Q and forgets to subtract 25Q²/2 · C quotes the equilibrium price rather than an area.

questions.q: 750 = 1000e^(0.035t) − 1000 gives an exhaustion year of
questions.why: Why B is right: e^(0.035t) = 1.75, so t = ln(1.75)/0.035 = 15.989 ≈ 16 years after 2005. Why the others are wrong: A divides by the slide's misprinted 0.0035, giving 159.89 years · C rounds 15.989 down to 15 · D multiplies by 0.035 instead of dividing.
